decisions.quote:
First, as claimed in RRP, the paper reported 18 items in the I/E values’ scale however, the data contained 19 items. To investigate further, the references mentioned in Ku & Zaroff (2014) against the scale were tracked. Therefore, Duriez et al (2007) and Unanue et al (2014) were tracked. Here, 18 items were reported. Therefore, the dataset was revised accordingly for the purpose of the reproduction (the 19th item’s data was deleted). 
Second, both Duriez et al (2007) and Unanue et al (2014) recommended reversing scores for the ‘Intrinsic’ items instead of ‘Extrinsic’ items (the latter was performed in Ku & Zaroff (2014)). To correct for this, in the reproduction, the ‘Intrinsic’ items were reversed. 
Third, in Ku & Zaroff (2014), the authors have reversed the signs for the ‘Extrinsic’ items instead of reverse scoring scores. To correct for this, in the reproduction, the items were reverse scored by subtracting the scores from 6 (as the rating scale ranged from 1-5).
decisions.reason: Working from the authors' original dataset (study 1 revision_1.sav), the analyst did not merely re-run original code unchanged: the analyst deleted a 19th scale item based on external references (Duriez et al., 2007; Unanue et al., 2014), reversed Intrinsic items instead of Extrinsic items, reverse-scored by subtracting from 6 rather than sign-flipping, and formed random SEM parcels. Those re-analyses yielded t = -5.12, p < .000 (vs. original t(79) = 4.87, p < .001 for single-trace) and standardized SEM path = .89, p < .000 (vs. original .54, p < .001 for m7k461). However, the short report evaluates results solely against 'Precise Reproduction Criteria' without stating whether the substantive hypotheses survive under the revised variable construction; the negative t sign cannot be inferred as a substantive reversal because SPSS group ordering and group means are unreported, while the SEM path remains positive and larger. Thus 'not checked' is too categorical and substantive survival is undeterminable.
